verses.text: I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with mirth: therefore enjoy pleasure”; and behold, this also was vanity.
I said of laughter, “It is foolishness”; and of mirth, “What does it accomplish?”

I searched in my heart how to cheer my flesh with wine, my heart yet guiding me with wisdom, and how to lay hold of folly, until I might see what it was good for the sons of men that they should do under heaven all the days of their lives.
I made myself great works. I built myself houses. I planted myself vineyards.
I made myself gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of all kinds of fruit.
I made myself pools of water, to water from it the forest where trees were reared.
I bought male servants and female servants, and had servants born in my house. I also had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all who were before me in Jerusalem;

I also gathered silver and gold for myself, and the treasure of kings and of the provinces. I got myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men — musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
So I was great, and increased more than all who were before me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also remained with me.
Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.
Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
I turned myself to consider wisdom, madness, and folly: for what can the king’s successor do? Just that which has been done long ago.
Then I saw that wisdom excels folly, as far as light excels darkness.
The wise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool walks in darkness — and yet I perceived that one event happens to them all.
Then I said in my heart, “As it happens to the fool, so will it happen even to me; and why was I then more wise?” Then I said in my heart that this also is vanity.
For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no memory for ever, since in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. Indeed, the wise man must die just like the fool!
So I hated life, because the work that is worked under the sun was grievous to me; for all is vanity and a chasing after wind.
I hated all my labor in which I labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
Who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have rule over all of my labor in which I have labored, and in which I have shown myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
Therefore I began to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor in which I had labored under the sun.
For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, with knowledge, and with skillfulness; yet he shall leave it for his portion to a man who has not labored for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.
For what has a man of all his labor, and of the striving of his heart, in which he labors under the sun?
For all his days are sorrows, and his travail is grief; yes, even in the night his heart takes no rest. This also is vanity.
There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?

For to the man who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he gives travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him who pleases God. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

footnotes.content: Here the Preacher turns to test mirth itself—as if joy could be chased and caught like a wild thing. He has decided to make pleasure his teacher, but notice how the experiment is bracketed: he'll test it, then find it empty. The Lord always knows what we'll find at the end of the tunnel before we walk into it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laughter is the surface; his question cuts beneath it—what work does merriment do? This is the sober voice asking sober questions. It sounds like the words of someone who has laughed hollow, whose mirth carried no freight. That honest reckoning is the beginning of wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He brings wine into the frame—the ancient symbol of pleasure. But mark the phrase: his heart yet guides him with wisdom even as he reaches for folly. He is not abandoned to his appetite; he watches himself experiment, as if from a distance. A careful man trying to understand what drives the sons of men.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Great works, houses, vineyards—these are the marks of a king, surely Solomon himself. The repetition of 'I made myself' almost rings hollow, doesn't it? Each declaration is a kind of reaching, as if naming all he's built might prove something.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gardens and parks, orchards of every fruit—a man planting to feed others, to create beauty and plenty. How tender it is, this impulse to make something pleasant flourish. Yet even gardens cannot stop time or satisfy the hunger that drives a king to build them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pools of water to feed the forest—a marvel of engineering, a gift that keeps giving. He is trying to make something permanent, something that outlasts his own hand. We know how that turns out, don't we? But the reaching itself deserves a quiet respect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Servants born in his house, herds and flocks beyond measure—wealth that speaks across generations. He is building an empire of presence, a kingdom that depends on him. But power like this carries its own weight; the more you have, the more will need managing after you leave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver, gold, treasure, singers, musical instruments—the catalog reads like the inventory of a temple. He gathers sensory delight itself: music, the sound of strings and pipe. Solomon, in his wisdom, reached for every taste the world offers. Did they feed him?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Great, increased, and still possessing wisdom—he has not lost his mind in pleasure. He stands at the pinnacle, looking down. Yet the saddest thing about being at the top is that you can see there is nothing beyond it but the view.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whatever his eyes desired, he took. His heart rejoiced. For a moment he had it all—the abundance he'd built poured out just for him. This is the dream almost every person harbors: enough room, enough things, enough joy to last. He lived it. And then?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All was vanity and a chasing after wind—the turning point. Readers today hear an echo in this: a man standing in his own kingdom, surveying what his hands have built, finding it empty. We see him looking at us across the centuries, teaching by his emptiness what gold never could. Christ alone is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He turns to wisdom and madness as if they were rooms to explore. What can come after the king? Only what came before. He is beginning to see that there are no new paths, only the same roads worn deep by a thousand feet before him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness—a simple, stark comparison. At least wisdom sees; at least it illuminates. Yet he will soon ask: does it help? Does the light save you if we all end the same?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wise man sees; the fool stumbles in darkness. And yet—the dreaded 'yet'—one event happens to them all. Death does not ask whether you had light or walked blind. It comes for the perceptive and the stumbling both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He feels the sting of it: if wisdom and folly end the same, why was he more wise? It's a human cry, almost angry. The Preacher is no longer serene; he's wrestling. This is closer to our own wrestling with the silence of God in suffering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wise or fool, there is no remembrance forever—both sink into the dust. This is Sheol's truth: even the great are forgotten. Yet the gospel speaks of a remembrance that does not fade, a Father who numbers even the hairs of our head. That changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He has moved from testing to hating—the work itself becomes grievous. This is the weight of chasing after wind: it leaves you exhausted, bitter, your hands empty even if your storehouses are full. Only a rest in God can set that right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He must leave it all to someone else—the succession that mocks every builder. He gives his life to something he cannot keep. This is the deepest bitterness of human toil, that we labor for something we must leave behind without choosing who finds it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Will the heir be wise or foolish? There is no knowing. The labor he labored so hard to lay down might go to someone who squanders it, or someone who builds on it. Life has no guarantees beyond this: we cannot control what comes after us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His heart begins to despair—the first moment when he lets the weight rest on him fully, without the shield of philosophy. This is a true dark night: the realization that all his striving, for all its success, could not buy one thing of lasting worth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A laborer with skill and wisdom works hard, and then leaves it to someone who didn't earn it. It seems grotesque, a cosmic injustice. He names it not only vanity but great evil. The order of the world rankles against our sense of what's right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What profit has a man from all his labor? The question is direct, almost brutal. He is asking the question that every honest person finally must ask: After all the work, all the striving, all the gathering—am I any closer to what matters?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His days are sorrows; even at night his heart finds no rest. The picture is of a man who has won the world and lost his peace. He carries his kingdom into his sleep. How close this comes to what Jesus saw in the hearts of the wealthy and driven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nothing better than to eat, drink, and let the soul enjoy good in labor—the turning. After all the wrestling and despair, he finds a smaller peace. Food, drink, the quietness of work done well, received as from God's hand. This is not pleasure chased, but pleasure received.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who can eat or enjoy more than he? Not more things, but more than Solomon—this seems to ask: can anyone surpass him? No, and that includes you and me. If it wasn't enough for him, what makes us think it will be for us?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To the one who pleases God, He gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy. To the sinner, toil and gathering that means nothing—a stark division. The Preacher has been learning that life goes differently depending on whether you are at peace with God. We have the answer to that now: Christ reconciles us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
